passage:
“Kunal, why is the remote in two pieces?”
Kunal, five, looked at the floor. “The cat did it.”
Yogesh raised his eyebrows. “Kunal. We don't have a cat.”
Kunal's cheeks went pink. He twisted his T-shirt. “Maybe a cat came in the window.”
“Beta, if you tell me what really happened, I won't be angry.”
A long pause. “I was jumping on the sofa. It fell.”
Yogesh knelt down. “Thank you for telling me the truth. Now I know I can believe you. Let's fix it together.”

qa.q: What did Kunal first say broke the remote?
qa.a: He said the cat did it.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel when his father said they don't have a cat?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and nervous, with pink cheeks, twisting his T-shirt.

qa.q: Why was Yogesh's response a good one?
qa.a: He stayed calm, thanked Kunal for the truth and explained that it helps him believe Kunal, so honesty felt safe.

qa.q: What would change if Yogesh had shouted as soon as Kunal lied?
qa.a: Kunal might have kept lying out of fear instead of learning that telling the truth builds trust.

grounding: A five-year-old tries a lie, is gently caught, and learns that truth keeps trust.

passage:
Class note, Thursday. Teacher: Charu.
On Monday, Tarun (five) told me he had finished his milk. Later I found the full cup behind the plant pot. I told him I felt sad that he didn't tell me the truth.
Today, Tarun said he had washed his hands, and his friend Veer said, “No, you didn't, you lie.” Tarun's face crumpled and he cried, “I did!” His hands were wet. He had.
Next step: we talked at circle time about how lies make it hard for people to believe us, even when we're telling the truth.

qa.q: Where did the teacher find Tarun's milk?
qa.a: The teacher found the full cup behind the plant pot.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when Veer didn't believe him?
qa.a: He felt hurt and upset, crying because he was telling the truth.

qa.q: Why was the circle-time talk a good next step?
qa.a: It helped all the children see that lies make it hard to be believed later.

qa.q: How might Veer see Tarun after the milk lie?
qa.a: Veer didn't trust Tarun's words, remembering the earlier lie.

grounding: A teacher notes a five-year-old learning that a lie makes it hard to be believed later.

passage:
In their village near Kolhapur, Leela, five, knocked Aai's clay water pot off the step. It cracked.
When Aai came, Leela pointed at her brother. “Tejas did it.”
Tejas, eight, got a scolding. He looked at Leela, hurt, but said nothing.
That evening, Leela shouted that Tejas took her ribbon. Aai didn't listen. “Are you sure, Leela?”
Leela's lip wobbled. She whispered, “I broke the pot. Not Tejas.”
Aai hugged Tejas. Then she held Leela's hand. “Thank you for telling me. Now say sorry to your brother.”

qa.q: What did Leela knock off the step?
qa.a: She knocked Aai's clay water pot off the step.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when Aai didn't listen to her about the ribbon?
qa.a: She felt upset and guilty, her lip wobbling, because she knew she had lied before.

qa.q: What did Aai do that helped Leela learn?
qa.a: She thanked Leela for finally telling the truth and asked her to say sorry to her brother.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when he was scolded for Leela's lie?
qa.a: He felt hurt and unfairly blamed, but stayed quiet.

grounding: A five-year-old sees how her lie stops her mother believing her, and tells the truth.

passage:
In the kindergarten in Helsinki, Paulo, five, ran past the block corner and knocked down Sami's tall tower.
Sami's face crumpled. “My tower!”
Paulo stopped. He looked at the blocks on the floor and at Sami's tears.
“Sorry,” he said. “It was an accident.”
Sami still cried.
Paulo knelt down. “I'll help build it again. Bigger.”
He handed Sami a red block. Sami sniffed and took it. Soon the tower was taller than before.

qa.q: What did Paulo knock down?
qa.a: He knocked down Sami's tall tower.

qa.q: How did Paulo feel when he saw Sami crying?
qa.a: He felt sorry and a bit guilty, so he stopped and apologised.

qa.q: What did Paulo do besides saying sorry, and why did it help?
qa.a: He helped rebuild the tower, which showed he really wanted to fix the harm.

qa.q: How did Sami feel when Paulo handed him a block?
qa.a: He began to feel better and less upset, accepting Paulo's help.

grounding: A five-year-old repairs an accident by apologising and helping rebuild.

passage:
In the school library, Divyansh, five, was turning pages too fast. Rrrip. A page of the elephant book tore halfway.
He looked around. Nobody had seen. He could put it back on the shelf.
Instead he carried it to the desk. “Ma'am, I tore it. Sorry.”
Ms Parul looked at the page, then at him. “Thank you for telling me. Shall we fix it?”
She gave him the tape. Divyansh stuck it very carefully, tongue between his teeth.

qa.q: Which book did Divyansh tear?
qa.a: He tore a page of the elephant book.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel when he tore the page?
qa.a: He felt worried and guilty, looking around to see if anyone had seen.

qa.q: How did Ms Parul help Divyansh make amends?
qa.a: She thanked him for telling and let him fix the page with tape himself.

qa.q: How might Ms Parul feel about Divyansh's honesty?
qa.a: She likely feels pleased and proud that he told the truth instead of hiding it.

grounding: A five-year-old admits tearing a library book and helps repair it.

passage:
I'm Aditi, Tarun's big sister. On Sunday I saw him come home from the neighbour's with Chintu's toy car in his pocket.
At dinner he was very quiet. He kept touching his pocket.
After dinner he got his crayons and drew a car with a big heart. He wrote a wobbly “SORY.”
Then he asked me to walk with him next door. He gave Chintu the car and the drawing. “I took it. Sorry.”
Chintu grinned and let him play with it for five minutes.

qa.q: What did Tarun draw?
qa.a: He drew a car with a big heart.

qa.q: Why was Tarun quiet at dinner?
qa.a: He probably felt guilty and uneasy about taking Chintu's car.

qa.q: What was good about how Tarun made amends?
qa.a: He returned the car, said sorry and gave a drawing, repairing the harm in more than one way.

qa.q: How did Chintu react to Tarun's apology?
qa.a: Chintu was happy and forgiving, grinning and sharing the car with Tarun.

grounding: An older sister observes her little brother return a taken toy and apologise.

passage:
I'm Vasudha. On the bus to Pune station I sat behind a little boy called Sumit, five, and his mother. A man in a wheelchair was near the door.
Sumit stared, then said loudly, “Mummy, why does that uncle have wheels?”
His mother went red. But the man smiled. “My legs don't walk, so my chair walks for me.”
Sumit thought. “Can it go fast?”
“Very fast.”
“Cool,” said Sumit, and waved when the man got off.

qa.q: What did the man say about his chair?
qa.a: He said his legs don't walk, so his chair walks for him.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when he asked about the wheels?
qa.a: He was curious and interested, not unkind.

qa.q: What could Sumit's mother say to him after the ride?
qa.a: She could say that asking kindly is okay and that people's bodies work in different ways.

qa.q: How might the man in the wheelchair feel about Sumit's question?
qa.a: He likely didn't mind, since Sumit was curious and friendly, and he answered with a smile.

grounding: A passenger observes a five-year-old noticing a man's wheelchair with curiosity, not hostility.

passage:
Monday: A new girl, Nandini, joined Sahil's class. She spoke Tamil with her mother at the gate. Sahil, five, whispered, “She talks funny.”
Ms Farida said, “She speaks Tamil. You speak Hindi. Both are good.”
Wednesday: Nandini taught the class to say “vanakkam.” Sahil said it too, laughing.
Next Monday: Sahil ran to Nandini at the gate. “Vanakkam!” She giggled. “Namaste!” They went inside holding hands.

qa.q: What word did Nandini teach the class?
qa.a: She taught the class to say “vanakkam.”

qa.q: How did Sahil feel about Nandini by next Monday?
qa.a: He felt friendly and happy, running to greet her.

qa.q: What did Ms Farida say that helped Sahil?
qa.a: She explained that Nandini speaks Tamil and that both languages are good, turning the difference into something normal.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel when Sahil greets her in Tamil?
qa.a: She probably feels welcome and happy, giggling and greeting him back.

grounding: Over a week a five-year-old moves from calling a new girl's language funny to greeting her in it.

passage:
It was pouring at pickup time, and Minakshi's umbrella was the only one left by the school gate.
Minakshi, five, saw Damini's Nani arrive, soaked. “Where's your mummy, Damini?”
“I live with Nani,” Damini said.
Minakshi thought. “Oh. My Nani lives with us. She makes laddoos.”
“Mine makes kheer.”
Minakshi held out her umbrella. “Share?”
The two girls squashed under it together, Nani holding her dupatta over her own head, laughing.

qa.q: Who arrived soaked at pickup time?
qa.a: Damini's Nani arrived soaked.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel on hearing that Damini lives with her Nani?
qa.a: She felt curious and accepting, finding something in common instead of judging.

qa.q: What could a teacher say to encourage this kind of kindness?
qa.a: A teacher could praise Minakshi for sharing and say that families come in many shapes.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Minakshi shares her umbrella?
qa.a: She probably feels included and happy, not made to feel different.

grounding: In the rain a five-year-old notices a different family type and responds kindly.

passage:
Monday: Ms Gurpreet asked each child in the class, “What's your name, and your mummy's phone number?” Sumit, five, knew his name but only the first two numbers.
Wednesday: Sumit's mother taught him the number as a song, clapping on each digit. He sang it in the bath.
Saturday: At the busy vegetable market, Sumit let go of his mother's hand to look at the parrots. When he turned around, she wasn't there.
He didn't run. He went to the fruit-seller's stall, said, “I'm Sumit. My mummy's number is…” and sang it. The fruit-seller called. His mother came running.

qa.q: What did Sumit do when he couldn't see his mother?
qa.a: He went to the fruit-seller's stall and said his name and sang his mummy's number.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt when he turned and his mother wasn't there?
qa.a: He probably felt scared, but he stayed calm enough to do what he had practised.

qa.q: Why was the number song a good idea?
qa.a: It made the phone number easy to remember, so Sumit could use it when he needed help.

qa.q: How did Sumit's mother feel when she came running?
qa.a: She was probably frightened and then very relieved to find him safe.

grounding: Over a week a five-year-old learns his mother's number and uses it when lost at the market.

passage:
The school bus was already at the stop across the busy road, and Kavitha, five, saw her friend waving from the window.
“Wait for me!” She tugged away from Gargi Mausi's hand.
Then she stopped. She remembered the rule.
“Mausi, hold hand,” she said, reaching back.
They stood at the crossing. Cars rushed past. The bus driver waited. When the green man came on, they crossed together.
“You remembered,” Gargi said, squeezing her hand.

qa.q: Who was waving from the bus window?
qa.a: Kavitha's friend was waving from the window.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel when she saw the bus and her friend?
qa.a: She felt excited and hurried, wanting to rush across.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do that kept her safe, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She stopped and took Gargi's hand to cross at the green man, because the road was busy with cars.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel when Kavitha remembers the rule?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and proud that Kavitha chose to be safe.

grounding: With a bus waiting, a five-year-old remembers to cross the road holding an adult's hand.

passage:
At bedtime, Kunal, five, pulled the sheet to his chin. “Mumma, the big boy at the play area touched me under my shorts. He said it's a secret. I didn't like it.”
Pallavi kept her voice soft. “Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing. It is not your fault.”
She listened to everything he wanted to say and told him he would not go down alone.
That same night she called the child helpline and told Kunal's papa. She also called the society secretary, who promised to speak to the boy's family the next morning.

qa.q: What did the big boy say about the touch?
qa.a: He said it's a secret.

qa.q: How was Kunal feeling when he told his mother?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and worried, pulling the sheet up to his chin because he didn't like the touch.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do that made her a safe adult to tell?
qa.a: She stayed calm, thanked him, said it was not his fault, listened, kept him safe and told the right people that same night.

qa.q: What would change if Pallavi had told Kunal not to make up stories?
qa.a: Kunal might stop telling her things, and the boy's behaviour would go unchecked, leaving Kunal and other children unprotected.

grounding: A five-year-old tells a trusted adult about unsafe touch, and his mother responds calmly and acts the same day.

passage:
In their Osaka flat, Jin, five, insisted on dressing himself for kindergarten.
He pulled on his trousers, then his shirt. He did up the buttons. Kaito, his father, watched from the doorway. The shirt was lopsided: one button in the wrong hole.
Jin looked in the mirror and frowned. “Wrong.” He undid them and started again, slowly, from the bottom.
This time it was straight.
“I did it!” he said.
Kaito smiled. “You did.”

qa.q: Where did Kaito watch from?
qa.a: He watched from the doorway.

qa.q: How did Jin feel when he saw his lopsided shirt, and then when he fixed it?
qa.a: He felt annoyed at first, frowning, and then proud when he did it right.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Kaito to only watch?
qa.a: It let Jin notice and fix the mistake himself, building his independence.

qa.q: What would change if Kaito had buttoned the shirt for Jin?
qa.a: Jin would have been ready faster, but he would have missed the pride of doing it himself.

grounding: A five-year-old dresses himself and fixes his own mistake.

passage:
At lunchtime in the school canteen, Ms Alka's class had a rule: wash hands, then try one bite of everything.
Ankita, five, washed her hands with soap, counting to ten like she'd learned. Then she looked at her plate. Rice, dal and something green and bumpy.
“Karela,” said Ms Alka. “Just one bite.”
Ankita made a face. She took the smallest bite. Chewed. “Bitter!”
“Yes, it's bitter. You tried it,” said Ms Alka.
Ankita ate her rice, then took one more tiny bite.

qa.q: What did Ankita count to while washing her hands?
qa.a: She counted to ten.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when she saw the karela?
qa.a: She felt reluctant and unsure, making a face at the green, bumpy vegetable.

qa.q: What makes the class's “one bite” rule helpful?
qa.a: It lets children try new foods without pressure to finish them.

qa.q: How does Ms Alka see Ankita's reaction to the karela?
qa.a: She accepts that it's bitter and praises Ankita for trying.

grounding: A five-year-old washes her hands independently and tries a new food at school.

passage:
I'm Gautam, Payal's cousin, staying with them for the holidays. I watched Payal, five, get ready for bed on her own.
She brushed her teeth, standing on a little stool, and spat carefully. She put on her pyjamas backwards, laughed, and turned them round. She folded her day clothes, badly, and put them on the chair.
Then she called, “Mumma, I'm ready!” and climbed into bed.
My little brother still needs help with everything. Payal seemed very proud.

qa.q: What did Payal stand on to brush her teeth?
qa.a: She stood on a little stool.

qa.q: How did Payal seem to feel when she called that she was ready?
qa.a: She seemed very proud of doing her bedtime routine herself.

qa.q: What could Payal's family do to support her independence?
qa.a: They could keep letting her do the steps herself and praise her effort, even when clothes are folded badly.

qa.q: How does Gautam see Payal's routine?
qa.a: Gautam is impressed, comparing it with a younger brother who still needs help.

grounding: A cousin observes a five-year-old independently brushing, dressing and getting to bed.

passage:
“Amma, the milk is going to spill!”
“Let it, Hemant. Watch.”
The milk in the new clay pot rose, foamed, and bubbled over the edge.
Bhavna and Paati clapped. “Pongalo Pongal!”
Hemant, five, clapped too. “Why do we let it spill?”
“So our year overflows with good things. That's how our family does it.”
“Every year?”
“Every year. My Paati did it too.”
Hemant shouted it again, louder. “Pongalo Pongal!”

qa.q: What did the milk bubble over?
qa.a: It bubbled over the edge of the new clay pot.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when everyone clapped?
qa.a: He felt excited and happy to be part of the celebration.

qa.q: How could Bhavna help Hemant learn more about the tradition?
qa.a: She could tell him stories of how her Paati celebrated and let him help with the next step.

qa.q: How might Paati feel hearing Hemant shout “Pongalo Pongal”?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and happy that the family tradition continues.

grounding: A five-year-old takes part in a family Pongal ritual and learns why they do it.

passage:
Class note, February. Teacher: Ishita.
Today Pema (five) told the class about Losar, her family's new year. She brought khapse, twisty fried biscuits her Ama had made.
She showed us how her family says “Tashi Delek” with hands together. “That's how we say happy new year at home,” she said, standing very straight.
The other children tried saying it. Pema corrected them, giggling.
Next step: I've invited Pema's Ama to tell a folk story next week.

qa.q: What did Pema bring for the class?
qa.a: She brought khapse, twisty fried biscuits her Ama had made.

qa.q: How did Pema seem to feel sharing her tradition?
qa.a: She seemed proud and confident, standing very straight.

qa.q: Why is inviting Pema's Ama a good next step?
qa.a: It brings Pema's family tradition into the classroom and helps all children learn about it.

qa.q: How might the other children feel learning to say “Tashi Delek”?
qa.a: They probably feel curious and enjoy learning something new from their classmate.

grounding: A teacher notes a five-year-old sharing her family's Losar traditions with pride.

passage:
On Ugadi morning in their village near Hassan, Mohit-thatha handed Harsha, five, a little leaf cup.
“Bevu-bella,” he said. “Neem and jaggery.”
Harsha tasted it. His face scrunched. “Bitter! And sweet!”
Thatha laughed. “Yes. That's how our family starts the new year. A little bitter, a little sweet, because the year will have both.”
Harsha tasted again, slower. “Thatha, next year can I make it?”
“Next year, you'll grind the jaggery.”

qa.q: What did Mohit-thatha hand Harsha?
qa.a: He handed him a little leaf cup of bevu-bella.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when he tasted the bevu-bella?
qa.a: He was surprised by the bitter and sweet taste, then curious and keen to help.

qa.q: How did Thatha help Harsha understand the tradition?
qa.a: He explained the meaning simply and promised Harsha a job next year.

qa.q: How might Thatha feel when Harsha asks to make it next year?
qa.a: He likely feels happy and proud that Harsha wants to carry on the tradition.

grounding: A five-year-old takes part in an Ugadi tradition and learns what it means in his family.

In their small town near Ujjain, Parveen-khala gave Mridul, five, her phone to watch a cartoon while she cooked.
When the timer rang, she said, “Phone time is over.”
Mridul whined. “One more!”
“No, beta. Timer said finish.”
He gave it back, pouting. Then he asked, “Khala, can dogs really fly like in the cartoon?”
“No. That's pretend. Real dogs run and bark.”
Mridul ran out to the lane to check on the neighbour's dog.

qa.q: What did Parveen-khala say when the timer rang?
qa.a: She said, “Phone time is over.”

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when he had to give the phone back?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and grumpy, pouting and whining.

qa.q: Why was using a timer helpful?

qa.q: How might Parveen-khala see Mridul's question about flying dogs?
qa.a: She likely finds it sweet and a good chance to explain pretend versus real.

passage:
In their São Paulo flat, an advert came on TV: a boy ate cereal and flew over the city.
Kaito, five, jumped up. “Mamãe, if I eat that, I can fly!”
Sofia laughed gently. “That's an advert. They make it look magic so people buy it. Nobody flies from cereal.”
“Never?”
“Never.”
Kaito thought. “Then they lied.”
“They pretended, to sell it.”
Kaito sat down, frowning at the TV. “Tricky.”

qa.a: He flew over the city.

qa.q: How did Kaito feel when he learned the truth about the advert?

qa.q: How did Sofia help Kaito understand adverts?

qa.q: How might Sofia feel about Kaito calling the advert tricky?
qa.a: She may feel pleased that he is beginning to think critically about adverts.

grounding: A five-year-old learns that adverts show pretend things to sell, not reality.

passage:
In Ms Rehana's class, Gautam, five, stood on a chair with his arms out. “I'm a superhero! I can fly!”

passage:
Class note. Teacher: Gargi.
For weeks, Irawati (five) needed three reminders at home time: shoes, bag, water bottle.
On Monday I stuck three small pictures by her hook: a shoe, a bag, a bottle.
Today she pointed at each picture and did each one, saying “Shoe. Bag. Bottle.” She was ready first. She told me, “I did all by myself!”
Next step: I'll add a fourth picture next week, her jumper.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when she was ready first?

passage:

Ritu, five, had a routine: shoes, bag, water bottle. She put on her shoes. She grabbed her bag. She ran to the door.
Then she stopped. “Bottle!”
She ran back to the kitchen table, grabbed it, and ran out.
Bidisha watched from the verandah. She hadn't said a word.
Ritu waved from the van, holding up the bottle.

qa.a: The school van honked at 7:40.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when she remembered her bottle?
qa.a: She felt a moment of worry and then pride as she ran back to get it.

qa.q: Why was it helpful that Bidisha didn't remind Ritu?

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel watching Ritu wave with the bottle?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and pleased that Ritu managed the routine alone.

passage:
In Mexico City, Alejandro sang the going-out song while he tied his own shoes. “Jacket, hat, and snack in bag!”
Nadia, five, sang it back. She pulled on her jacket, zipped it halfway, then all the way. She put on her hat. She looked around.
“Snack!”
She took the banana from the table and put it in her bag.
“Ready, Papá!”
Alejandro opened the door. “Park, here we come.”

qa.q: What was Nadia's snack?
qa.a: A banana from the table.

qa.q: How did Nadia feel when she said “Ready, Papá!”?
qa.a: She felt proud and excited to have done all the steps herself.

qa.q: Why was singing the going-out song helpful?
qa.a: The song put the steps in order, so Nadia could remember each one.

qa.q: How might Alejandro feel when Nadia is ready by herself?
qa.a: He probably feels pleased and proud, and happy they can leave quickly.

grounding: A five-year-old follows a sung three-step routine to get ready for the park.

passage:
Class note. Teacher: Sabina.
Nikita (five) asked me six times today, “Is it my birthday?” Her birthday is on Friday.
So I made a paper chain with three links. “Each morning, you tear one link. When there are no links, it's your birthday.”
She tore one today. “Yesterday I had four sleeps. Today three. Tomorrow two!” she said.
She didn't ask again all afternoon.
Next step: I'll use paper chains for the class trip next month.

qa.q: How many times did Nikita ask if it was her birthday?
qa.a: She asked six times today.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel about waiting for her birthday?
qa.a: She felt impatient and excited, asking again and again.

qa.q: Why did the paper chain help Nikita wait?
qa.a: It showed her the days in a way she could see and count, so waiting felt easier.

qa.q: How might the teacher feel when Nikita stops asking?
qa.a: The teacher probably feels relieved and pleased that the chain helped.

grounding: A teacher helps a five-year-old understand days until her birthday and wait calmly.

passage:
In their village near Amritsar, Gurleen, five, stood at the gate every evening. “Is Papa coming today?”
“Not today,” said Vandana. “The day after tomorrow.”
“Is that far?”
Vandana gave her two pebbles. “Throw one in the pot tonight, and one tomorrow night. Then Papa comes.”
That night Gurleen threw one. “Tomorrow, one more. Then Papa!”
She stopped waiting at the gate and went to feed the calf.

qa.q: How many pebbles did Vandana give Gurleen?
qa.a: She gave her two pebbles.

qa.q: How was Gurleen feeling as she stood at the gate each evening?
qa.a: She felt impatient and missed her Papa.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that helped Gurleen understand?
qa.a: She used pebbles to show the days, so Gurleen could see how long to wait.

passage:
In Prague, Tomas, five, woke up and asked Clara, “Is Babička coming today?”
Clara pointed to the calendar on the fridge. “Yesterday was Friday. Today is Saturday. Babička comes tomorrow, Sunday.”
Tomas looked at the calendar. He touched Friday, then Saturday, then Sunday.
“So one more sleep?”
“One more sleep.”
He sighed. “That's long.”
“Shall we bake her a cake today, so it's ready tomorrow?”
Tomas jumped up. “Yes!”

qa.q: When does Babička come?
qa.a: She comes tomorrow, Sunday.

qa.q: How did Tomas feel about waiting one more sleep?
qa.a: He felt impatient, sighing that it was long.

qa.q: How did Clara help Tomas with waiting?
qa.a: She showed him the days on the calendar and gave him a fun task for today.

qa.q: How might Babička feel when she sees the cake?
qa.a: She would probably feel happy and loved that Tomas prepared for her visit.

grounding: A five-year-old learns the order of days and waits for his grandmother's visit.

passage:
At the kindergarten in Berlin, Selin, five, always sat next to Abebe. They shared crayons and built the same castle every day.
On Tuesday Abebe didn't come. Selin kept looking at the door. She put her coat on his chair so nobody else would sit there.
“He's sick today,” said the teacher.
Selin drew a picture of their castle and wrote an A on it. “For Abebe. Tomorrow.”

qa.q: What did Selin put on Abebe's chair?
qa.a: She put her coat on his chair.

qa.q: How did Selin feel when Abebe didn't come?
qa.a: She missed him and felt a bit sad and worried, looking at the door.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Selin while Abebe is away?
qa.a: The teacher could let her keep the drawing for Abebe and invite her to play with others for a while.

qa.q: How might Abebe feel when he gets the drawing?
qa.a: He would probably feel happy and special that Selin missed him.

grounding: A five-year-old misses her chosen friend and saves his seat when he is absent.

passage:
At the school playground, Binita, five, only wanted to play with Naveen. She saved him a place in the line. She shared her tiffin.
On Friday, an older boy laughed at Naveen's glasses. “Four eyes!”
Binita stepped in front of Naveen. “Stop it! He's my friend.”
The older boy walked away.
Naveen whispered, “Thank you.” Binita held his hand all the way back to class.

qa.q: What did the older boy laugh at?
qa.a: He laughed at Naveen's glasses.

qa.q: How did Binita feel when the older boy laughed at Naveen?
qa.a: She felt angry and protective of her friend.

qa.q: What could a teacher do after the playground moment?
qa.a: A teacher could praise Binita for standing up kindly and speak to the older boy about teasing.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel when Binita stood up for him?
qa.a: He felt grateful and safer, whispering thank you.

grounding: A five-year-old shows loyalty to her chosen friend when he is teased.

passage:
I'm Salma, the neighbour. Last month Joseph's best friend, Kiran, moved to another city. Joseph is five.
For days after, Joseph sat on the stairs where they used to play marbles. He didn't want to play with anyone else.
One evening he asked me, “Aunty, how far is Chennai?”
“Very far.”
He went quiet. Then he said, “I'll draw Kiran a picture so he doesn't forget me.”
Yesterday I saw his mother posting it.

qa.q: Where did Joseph sit after Kiran moved?
qa.a: He sat on the stairs where they used to play marbles.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel after Kiran moved away?
qa.a: He felt sad and lonely, missing his best friend.

qa.q: How could Joseph's family help him with missing Kiran?
qa.a: They could help him send pictures or talk on the phone, and gently invite him to play with other children.

qa.q: How does Salma see Joseph's feelings?
qa.a: Salma notices his sadness and is touched by how he wants Kiran not to forget him.

grounding: A neighbour observes a five-year-old missing his chosen friend and showing loyalty.
